summary: I independently recomputed git hash-object over every file under compiler/ and reproduced all 24 entries of COMPILER_FREEZE.txt exactly; RUNTIME_FREEZE.txt (13) and KERNEL_FREEZE.txt (5) also reproduce exactly, and `git diff origin/main HEAD -- compiler/` is empty, so the compiler is genuinely frozen rather than re-frozen after edits (COMPILER_FREEZE.txt has one commit in its history, b84362d, and the last commit touching compiler/, 746191e, predates it). The runtime genuinely consumes the compiler's real output: across 373 scene manifests on disk every one has exactly the four fields, all 807 actor objects have exactly {name, private_context}, and every compiled_scene.json in simulations_v3 and matched_pairs is byte-identical to the compiler's own final_scene_manifest.json with matching question/start/cutoff. There is no second compiler, WorldSpec, World, Clock, EventQueue, journal store or replay path anywhere in the repo. Three gaps remain, all latent rather than actual: KERNEL_FREEZE covers only 5 of the 9 kernel modules the production compiler reaches, run_simulation.py --scene accepts any JSON as a 'frozen compiler artifact' without validation or provenance, and a .pyc under compiler/__pycache__/ evades the freeze entirely - I demonstrated all three empirically in a throwaway copy.

findings.title: KERNEL_FREEZE.txt omits the kernel modules the production compiler actually imports and uses
findings.evidence: artifacts/semantic_runtime/KERNEL_FREEZE.txt lists only engine.py, events.py, simclock.py, terminals.py, world.py. But compiler/scene_adapter.py:28 does `from sworldmodel import ActorState, AttentionRule, World` and compiler/scene_pipeline.py:26 does `from sworldmodel import canonical_json` - so the production path executes sworldmodel/__init__.py (unfrozen) and uses ActorState from sworldmodel/actors.py:61 (unfrozen) and AttentionRule from sworldmodel/info.py:42 (unfrozen); __init__.py also pulls in actions.py and checkpoint.py, both unfrozen. ActorState is used at compiler/scene_adapter.py:74-79 and its to_dict() feeds w.apply("actor.add", ...), which feeds world.state_hash(), which compile_scene gates on at compiler/scene_pipeline.py:188-191 (INSTANTIATION_NOT_DETERMINISTIC) and 210-213 (REPLAY_MISMATCH). Demonstrated in a throwaway copy: injecting one extra key into ActorState.to_dict() in sworldmodel/actors.py changed the compiler's instantiated world hash from 5727a024c5e4696a... to 73ce83285afb567e..., changed the runtime's own actor.add ledger record via sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/adapter.py:24+76, and tests/test_compiler_runtime_integration.py::test_frozen_compiler_files_are_unchanged still reported '1 passed'.
findings.why_it_matters: The freeze test's own comment at tests/test_compiler_runtime_integration.py:193-195 states its purpose as closing exactly this hole - 'freezing compiler/ alone would leave the ground it stands on free to move' - but it leaves four of the nine reachable kernel modules free to move. Because sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/adapter.py imports ActorState from the same place, the same edit also silently changes every run's ledger and every replay hash while test_the_runtime_is_frozen_for_the_unseen_case (tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1436) stays green, so neither 'the compiler is frozen' nor 'the unseen case was run against exactly this implementation' is actually enforced end to end.
findings.suggested_fix: Add sworldmodel/__init__.py, actors.py, info.py, actions.py and checkpoint.py to KERNEL_FREEZE.txt, and derive the frozen set from the compiler's actual import closure rather than a hand-written list.

findings.title: run_simulation.py --scene accepts any JSON as a 'frozen compiler artifact', unvalidated and unrecorded
findings.evidence: run_simulation.py:54-60 does `scene = json.load(f)` on an arbitrary path, reads question/start/cutoff from a sibling input.json, prints '[compile] reusing frozen compiler artifact {path}' unconditionally, and passes the dict straight to instantiate_scene_manifest. compiler.scene_schema.validate_manifest_shape is never called on that path, no hash is compared against any compiler output, and the artifacts written for the run (trace.py:89-93, compile_runtime_bindings.json) record only consumed_fields - never which compiler artifact the manifest came from. This is the path that produced every run in artifacts/simulations_v3/ (none has a compile/ subdirectory) and 12 of the 17 matched-pair runs (the __r2/__r3/__r4 repeats).
findings.why_it_matters: The module docstring at run_simulation.py:11-12 claims 'still the compiler's own artifact, never a hand-authored world', but nothing in code establishes that - the guarantee rests entirely on the operator typing the right path. For a system whose governing rule is that code owns persistence and identity, the entire evidence base for the final evaluation reaches the world through an unvalidated JSON side door. I verified by canonical-JSON hash that in every actual run the manifest IS byte-identical to the compiler's own final_scene_manifest.json, so no violation occurred - but a reviewer cannot tell that from the run's own artifacts.
findings.suggested_fix: On the --scene path, run validate_manifest_shape and record the source path plus a hash of the manifest (and of the compiler artifact it matches) into compile_runtime_bindings.json.

findings.title: A .pyc under compiler/__pycache__/ replaces frozen compiler code with every freeze check green
findings.evidence: tests/test_compiler_runtime_integration.py:165-169 walks compiler/ collecting only files ending in .py and explicitly skips any path containing __pycache__; the untracked check at line 181-184 uses --exclude-standard, and .gitignore lines 1-2 ignore __pycache__/ and *.pyc. Demonstrated in a throwaway copy: compiling a modified compiler/scene_prompts.py to compiler/__pycache__/scene_prompts.cpython-311.pyc with PycInvalidationMode.UNCHECKED_HASH and then restoring the original .py byte-for-byte gave `from compiler import scene_prompts; scene_prompts.CALL1_SYSTEM[:60]` == 'BACKDOORED PROMPT. You are the scene compiler of an evidence', while test_frozen_compiler_files_are_unchanged reported '1 passed' and `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard compiler/` returned empty. As due diligence I checked the real repo: every .pyc under compiler/ is timestamp-validated and matches its current source, so nothing is hiding there today.
findings.why_it_matters: The freeze proves the compiler's source text is unchanged, not that the code Python executes is unchanged. The compiler loads no data files (the only open() calls in compiler/*.py are writes plus instantiate_compiled's two reads), so bytecode is the only non-.py surface - but it is a complete one: the entire two-call prompt doctrine lives in scene_prompts.py.
findings.suggested_fix: Have the freeze test assert that no .pyc exists under compiler/ that is hash-based or whose timestamp/size header does not match its source, or simply run the suite with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE and assert compiler/__pycache__ is absent.
